title: The Bay Area Memespace Map That Won’t Die
summary:
Juiciest bit: Qiaochu Yuan tried to reframe the whole rationalist/EA/x-risk scene as “essentially a parasite on Silicon Valley,” arguing it latched onto an “ideological vacuum” created when tech weirdos suddenly had huge salaries and no story for what to do with them. Eshear pushed back that “parasite” is needlessly accusatory—EA is “the call… from inside the house,” basically Bay Area tech culture’s philanthropy-shaped shadow (bed nets instead of museum galas). Visa chimed in with a link to Julia Galef’s original “Map of Bay Area memespace” like, look, we literally have a diagram for how this stuff grew here.

The whole strand starts way more wholesome: in 2019 Prigoose resurfaced Galef’s 2019 map (“Still love @juliagalef’s map of the Bay Area memespace”), and Visakanv immediately turned it into a personal challenge—“what my own memespace is like”—then live-posted increasingly deranged/beautiful iterations of his own “memex” diagram (“everything is connected,” “Make Friends. It is dangerous to go alone,” “One must imagine Sisyphus LOL-ing”), culminating in a dense final version that got him a flood of DMs and later, absurdly, a requested PDF. It even mutates into a meme format (the arms-outstretched guy surrounded by his mindmap). After that, the map mostly becomes evergreen reference material: Rhys Lindmark calls it “Evergreen content,” people share it as a starting point for understanding Bay Area communities, and xsphi snipes that it’s funny “hacker culture/open source culture are completely unrelated from computer scientists. Explains a lot.”

What peaked was Visa’s creative “make your own memespace” riff; what died was any real attempt to update or critique the underlying map—until Qiaochu’s “parasite” provocation briefly forces people to argue about whether EA is an outsider infection or native Bay Area output. And even then, the debate ends in citation, not synthesis. Why care: this is basically a cheat-sheet for how Bay Area ideology reproduces itself—how a single “map” becomes a cultural Rosetta Stone, a meme template, and then a proxy battleground for whether the whole ecosystem is admirable self-mythology or just tech money trying to buy meaning.
